competition: Czech-Polish-Slovak Mathematics Match (from 2019 Czech-Austrian-Polish-Slovak Match, CAPS)

problems.problem: The sequence of numbers $a_1, a_2, \ldots$ satisfies the condition $$a_{n+2}=(2-n^2)a_{n+1}+(2+n^2)a_n$$ for every integer $n\ge 1$, where $a_1=2$ and $a_2=5$. Decide whether there exist indices $p$, $q$ and $r$ such that $a_p\cdot a_q=a_r$.

Let $\mathbb{Z}$ denote the set of all integers. Find all pairs of functions $f, g\colon \mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}$ such that the equality $$f\bigl(g(x)+y\bigr)=g\bigl(f(y)+x\bigr)$$ holds for all integers $x$ and $y$, where $g(x)=g(y)$ if and only if $x=y$.

In the plane with a Cartesian coordinate system, consider all triangles $ABC$ whose vertices are lattice points (points with integer coordinates) and whose interior contains exactly one lattice point $P$. Let $E$ be the intersection of the side $BC$ with the line $AP$. Determine the largest possible value of the ratio $$\frac{|AP|}{|PE|}.$$
For every real number $p$ ($p>1$) determine the smallest value of the sum $x+y$, where the numbers $x$ and $y$ satisfy the equation $$\bigl(x+\sqrt{1+x^2}\bigr)\bigl(y+\sqrt{1+y^2}\bigr)=p.$$

A convex quadrilateral $ABCD$ is given whose diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ are perpendicular to each other. Prove that the images of the intersection point of the diagonals under the reflections in the sides of the quadrilateral $ABCD$ lie on one circle.
Find all pairs of nonnegative integers $x$ and $y$ that satisfy the equation $$p^x-y^p=1,$$ where $p$ is a given odd prime.

Let $\mathbb{Z}^*$ be the set of all nonzero integers. Prove that an integer $p>3$ is a prime if and only if for every pair of numbers $a, b\in\mathbb{Z}^*$ exactly one of the numbers $$N_1=a+b-6ab+\frac{p-1}{6},\qquad N_2=a+b+6ab+\frac{p+1}{6}$$ lies in the set $\mathbb{Z}^*$.

On a nonempty set $M$ an operation $*$ is given which assigns to every ordered pair of elements $(a,b)\in M	imes M$ some element $c\in M$, which we denote $c=a*b$. Consider operations $*$ with the property that the relations $$(a*b)*b=a\qquad	ext{and}\qquad a*(a*b)=b$$ hold for all elements $a, b\in M$.

a) Prove that every such operation is commutative, i.e. the equality $a*b=b*a$ holds for all $a, b\in M$.

b) On which finite sets $M$ does such an operation exist?

A regular quadrilateral pyramid has base edge length $2a$ and lateral edge length $a\sqrt{17}$. A point $M$ is chosen inside the pyramid. Consider the $5$ pyramids similar to the given one which have their apex at the point $M$ and whose bases lie in the planes of the faces of the given pyramid. Prove that the sum of the surface areas of these pyramids is greater than or equal to one fifth of the surface area of the given pyramid. Where must the point $M$ be chosen for equality to occur?

Let $\mathbb{Z}$ denote the set of all integers. Decide whether there exists a function $f\colon\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}$ such that for every $k=0, 1, 2, \ldots, 1996$ and for every $m\in\mathbb{Z}$ the equation $f(x)+k\cdot x=m$ has at least one solution $x$ in the integers.

Two sets of intervals $\mathcal{A}$ and $\mathcal{B}$ are given on a line. The set $\mathcal{A}$ contains $2m-1$ intervals, where $m\in\mathbb{N}$, no two intervals of $\mathcal{A}$ are disjoint or have only an endpoint in common, and every interval of $\mathcal{A}$ contains at least two disjoint intervals of $\mathcal{B}$. Prove that one can find an interval in $\mathcal{B}$ which belongs to at least $m$ intervals of $\mathcal{A}$.

Points $E$ and $D$ are chosen in the interiors of the sides $AC$ and $BC$, respectively, of a triangle $ABC$. Let $F$ be the intersection of the lines $AD$ and $BE$. Prove that the areas of the triangles $ABC$ and $ABF$ satisfy $$\frac{S_{ABC}}{S_{ABF}}=\frac{|AC|}{|AE|}+\frac{|BC|}{|BD|}-1.$$

An equilateral triangle $ABC$ is given. Points $K$ and $L$ are chosen on its sides $AB$ and $AC$, respectively, so that $|BK|=|AL|$. Let $P$ be the intersection of the segments $BL$ and $CK$. Determine the ratio $|AK|:|BK|$ if you know that the segments $AP$ and $CK$ are perpendicular to each other.

In a certain community of more than six people, every member corresponds with exactly three other members. Prove that this community can be divided into two nonempty groups so that every member corresponds with at least two members of the group to which he himself belongs.
Find all functions $f\colon\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ such that the equality $$f\bigl(f(x)+y\bigr)=f(x^2-y)+4f(x)y$$ holds for all pairs of real numbers $x$, $y$.
Is it possible to place $100$ balls in space, no two of which have a common interior point, in such a way that each of them touches at least one third of the others?

The sum of several integers (some of which may be equal) equals the number $1492$. Decide whether the sum of their seventh powers can equal

a) the number $1996$,

b) the number $1998$.

In a certain language there are only two letters, $A$ and $B$. The words of this language satisfy:

1) The only word of length $1$ is $A$.

2) An arbitrary group of letters $X_1X_2X_3\ldots X_nX_{n+1}$, where $X_i\in\{A,B\}$ for every index $i$, forms a word of length $n+1$ if and only if it contains at least one letter $A$ and at the same time is not of the form $X_1X_2\ldots X_nA$, where $X_1X_2\ldots X_n$ is a word of length $n$.

Prove that there are exactly $$ inom{3995}{1997}-1$$ words which do not begin with the pair of letters $AA$ and consist of $1998$ letters $A$ and the same number of letters $B$.
Let $P$ be an interior point of a parallelogram $ABCD$. Prove that $|\angle APB|+|\angle CPD|=180^\circ$ if and only if $|\angle PDC|=|\angle PBC|$.

A polynomial $P(x)$ of degree $n$, $n\ge 5$, with integer coefficients and with $n$ pairwise distinct integer roots is given. Find all integer roots of the polynomial $P(P(x))$ if you know that one of the roots of $P(x)$ is $0$.
In a convex hexagon $ABCDEF$ we have $|AB|=|BC|$, $|CD|=|DE|$ and $|EF|=|FA|$. Prove that then $$\frac{|BC|}{|BE|}+\frac{|DE|}{|DA|}+\frac{|FA|}{|FC|}\ge\frac{3}{2}.$$

Let $\mathbb{N}=\{1,2,3,\ldots\}$ denote the set of positive integers. Find all functions $f\colon\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}\setminus\{1\}$ such that $$f(n)+f(n+1)=f(n+2)\cdot f(n+3)-168\qquad\text{for every } n\in\mathbb{N}.$$
Let $T$ be the centroid of a triangle $ABC$ in which $|\angle TAB|=|\angle ACT|$. What is the largest value that the sum $$\sin|\angle CAT|+\sin|\angle CBT|$$ can attain?

In a camp there are $n$ girls $D_1, D_2, \ldots, D_n$ and $2n-1$ boys $C_1, C_2, \ldots, C_{2n-1}$. The girl $D_i$, $i=1, 2, \ldots, n$, knows exactly the boys $C_1, C_2, \ldots, C_{2i-1}$. Let $A(n,r)$ be the number of all possible ways of choosing $r$ ($r\ge 1$) pairs (boy - girl) from the children in the camp so that every chosen girl knows her boy in the pair. Prove that $$A(n,r)=\binom{n}{r}\cdot\frac{n!}{(n-r)!}.$$
Prove that for arbitrary positive numbers $a$, $b$, $c$ the inequality $$\frac{a}{b+2c}+\frac{b}{c+2a}+\frac{c}{a+2b}\ge 1$$ holds.

An acute triangle $ABC$ with altitudes $AD$, $BE$, $CF$ is given. Suppose that the lines $BC$ and $EF$ have a common point $P$, and that the line through the point $D$ parallel to $EF$ meets the line $AC$ at the point $Q$ and the line $AB$ at the point $R$. Prove that the circle circumscribed about the triangle $PQR$ passes through the midpoint of the side $BC$.

Determine all positive integers $k$ for which there exists a ten-element set $M$ of positive real numbers such that exactly $k$ different triangles have sides whose lengths are three (not necessarily distinct) elements of the set $M$. (Triangles that are not congruent are considered different.)

Find all positive integers $k$ for which the following holds: if $F(x)$ is an arbitrary polynomial with integer coefficients satisfying the inequalities $0\le F(c)\le k$ for every $c\in\{0, 1, \ldots, k+1\}$, then $F(0)=F(1)=\ldots=F(k+1)$.
Find all functions $f\colon(1,\infty)\to(-\infty,\infty)$ satisfying, for all numbers $x>1$ and $y>1$, the equation $$f(x)-f(y)=(y-x)f(xy).$$
Prove that for every positive integer $n\ge 3$ the least common multiple of the numbers $1, 2, \ldots, n$ is greater than the number $2^{n-1}$.
Prove that if positive real numbers $a$, $b$, $c$ satisfy the inequality $$5abc>a^3+b^3+c^3,$$ then there exists a triangle with side lengths $a$, $b$, $c$.

A triangle $ABC$ and its inscribed circle $k$ are given. Circles $k_a$, $k_b$, $k_c$ intersect the circle $k$ orthogonally, and the segments $BC$, $CA$, $AB$ are (in this order) their chords. The circles $k_a$, $k_b$ intersect for the second time at the point $C'$, the circles $k_c$, $k_a$ at the point $B'$ and the circles $k_b$, $k_c$ at the point $A'$. Prove that the radius of the circle circumscribed about the triangle $A'B'C'$ is half the radius of the circle $k$.\n\nRemark. Two circles are said to intersect orthogonally if their tangents at each common point are perpendicular to each other.
Let $n$ be a positive integer. Prove that $n$ is a power of $2$ if and only if there exists an integer $m$ such that $2^n-1$ is a divisor of $m^2+9$.
Let $P(x)$ be a polynomial with integer coefficients. Prove that then the polynomial $$Q(x)=P(x^4)P(x^3)P(x^2)P(x)+1$$ has no integer root.

Let $ABCD$ be an isosceles trapezoid with bases $AB$ and $CD$. The circle inscribed in the triangle $BCD$ touches the side $CD$ at the point $E$. Let $F$ be the point on the bisector of the angle $DAC$ such that the lines $EF$ and $CD$ are perpendicular to each other. The circle circumscribed about the triangle $ACF$ intersects the line $CD$ at the points $C$ and $G$. Prove that the triangle $AFG$ is isosceles.

Every integer is coloured with one of the colours red, blue, green and white. Let $x$ and $y$ be odd integers such that $|x|\ne|y|$. Prove that there exist two integers of the same colour whose difference takes one of the values $x$, $y$, $x+y$ or $x-y$.
Prove that for arbitrary positive numbers $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$ ($n\ge 2$) the inequality $$(a_1^3+1)(a_2^3+1)\ldots(a_n^3+1)\ge(a_1^2a_2+1)(a_2^2a_3+1)\ldots(a_n^2a_1+1)$$ holds.

A triangle $ABC$ has acute interior angles at the vertices $A$ and $B$. Isosceles triangles $ACD$ and $BCE$ with bases $AC$ and $BC$ are constructed externally on the sides $AC$ and $BC$ of the triangle so that $|\angle ADC|=|\angle ABC|$ and at the same time $|\angle BEC|=|\angle BAC|$. Let $S$ be the centre of the circle circumscribed about the triangle $ABC$. Prove that the length of the broken line $DSE$ equals the perimeter of the triangle $ABC$ if and only if the angle $ACB$ is a right angle.

For arbitrary positive integers $n$, $k$ satisfying the conditions $\frac{1}{2}n<k\le\frac{2}{3}n$, find the smallest number of squares that can be occupied on an $n\times n$ square chessboard so that in no row and in no column of the chessboard are there $k$ adjacent free (i.e. unoccupied) squares.

Points $A$, $B$ ($A
e B$) are given in the plane. In this plane consider an arbitrary triangle $ABC$ with the property: on its sides $BC$, $CA$ there exist, respectively, points $D$, $E$ for which

(i) $\dfrac{|BD|}{|BC|}=\dfrac{|CE|}{|CA|}=\dfrac{1}{3}$;

(ii) the points $A$, $B$, $D$, $E$ lie (in this order) on one circle.

Determine the set of intersection points of the lines $AD$ and $BE$ for all triangles $ABC$ with the given property.
Determine all functions $f\colon\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ satisfying the equation $$f(x^2+y)+f\bigl(f(x)-y\bigr)=2f\bigl(f(x)\bigr)+2y^2$$ for all $x, y\in\mathbb{R}$.

A Cartesian coordinate system is given in space. Every point with integer coordinates is called a lattice point. We colour $2000$ lattice points blue and another $2000$ lattice points red so that no two blue-red segments have a common interior point. (A segment is called blue-red if one of its endpoints is coloured blue and the other red.) Consider the smallest rectangular box with edges parallel to the coordinate axes which contains all the coloured points.

(a) Prove that the box contains at least $500\,000$ lattice points.

(b) Give an example of the described colouring for which the considered box contains at most $8\,000\,000$ lattice points.

A triangle $ABC$ with area $S$ is given. For its side lengths $|BC|=a$, $|CA|=b$, $|AB|=c$ we have $a\le b\le c$. Determine the largest real number $u$ and the smallest real number $v$ such that for every interior point $P$ of the triangle $ABC$ the inequality $$u\le|PD|+|PE|+|PF|\le v$$ holds, where $D$, $E$, $F$ are, respectively, the intersections of the lines $AP$, $BP$, $CP$ with the opposite sides of the given triangle. (Express the values $u$, $v$ in terms of the given quantities $a$, $b$, $c$ and $S$.)

Let $S=\{1, 2, \ldots, n\}$, where $n$ is a given positive integer. Determine the number of all functions $f\colon S\to S$ such that $x+f^4(x)=n+1$ for every $x\in S$. (The symbol $f^4$ denotes the fourth iterate, i.e. $f^4(x)=f(f(f(f(x))))$.)
Let $n>1$ be a positive integer and $p$ a prime such that $n$ is a divisor of $p-1$ and at the same time $p$ is a divisor of $n^3-1$. Prove that $4p-3$ is the square of a positive integer.

Let $O$ denote the centre of the circle circumscribed about an acute triangle $ABC$. Let $P$, $Q$ be points on its sides $AC$, $BC$, respectively, such that $$\frac{|AP|}{|PQ|}=\frac{|BC|}{|AB|}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\frac{|BQ|}{|PQ|}=\frac{|AC|}{|AB|}.$$ Prove that the points $O$, $P$, $Q$ and $C$ lie on one circle.

Let $n\ge 2$ be an even positive integer. Consider polynomials of the form $$P(x)=x^n+a_{n-1}x^{n-1}+\ldots+a_1x+1$$ with real coefficients which have at least one real root. Determine the smallest possible value of the sum $a_1^2+\ldots+a_{n-1}^2$.

Let $n\ge 2$ be a positive integer. Solve in the real numbers the system of equations $$\begin{aligned}\max\{1,x_1\}&=x_2,\\ \max\{2,x_2\}&=2x_3,\\ &\;\;\vdots\\ \max\{n-1,x_{n-1}\}&=(n-1)x_n,\\ \max\{n,x_n\}&=nx_1.\end{aligned}$$

If the numbers $p$, $q$, $r$ from the interval $\left[\frac{2}{5},\frac{5}{2}\right]$ satisfy $pqr=1$, then there exist two triangles with equal areas, one of which has sides $a$, $b$, $c$ and the other has sides $pa$, $qb$, $rc$. Prove it.

A triangle $ABC$ is given and inside it a point $P$ lying on the median from the vertex $C$. Let $X$ be the intersection of the line $AP$ with the side $BC$ and $Y$ the intersection of the line $BP$ with the side $AC$. Prove that if the quadrilateral $ABXY$ is cyclic, then the triangle $ABC$ is isosceles.
Determine all positive integers $n\ge 2$ for which all the binomial coefficients $$\binom{n}{1},\ \binom{n}{2},\ \ldots,\ \binom{n}{n-1}$$ are even numbers.
Find all functions $f\colon\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ which for all $x, y\in\mathbb{R}$ satisfy the relation $$f\bigl(f(x)+y\bigr)=2x+f\bigl(f(y)-x\bigr).$$

Prove that real numbers $p$, $q$, $r$ satisfy the condition $$p^4(q-r)^2+2p^2(q+r)+1=p^4$$ if and only if the quadratic equations $$x^2+px+q=0,\qquad y^2-py+r=0$$ have real roots (not necessarily distinct) which can be labelled $x_{1,2}$ and $y_{1,2}$, respectively, in such an order that the equality $x_1y_1-x_2y_2=1$ holds.

Prove that for every positive integer $k$ there exist at most finitely many triples of pairwise distinct primes $p$, $q$, $r$ for which the number $qr-k$ is a multiple of $p$, the number $pr-k$ is a multiple of $q$ and at the same time the number $pq-k$ is a multiple of $r$.

Inside a cyclic quadrilateral $ABCD$ a point $P$ is given such that $$|\angle BPC|=|\angle BAP|+|\angle PDC|.$$ Let $E$, $F$, $G$ be the feet of the perpendiculars from the point $P$ to the lines $AB$, $AD$ and $DC$, respectively. Prove that the triangle $FEG$ is similar to the triangle $PBC$.
Solve in the real numbers the system of equations $$\frac{1}{xy}=\frac{x}{z}+1,\qquad \frac{1}{yz}=\frac{y}{x}+1,\qquad \frac{1}{zx}=\frac{z}{y}+1.$$

Points $K$, $L$, $M$ are chosen in the interiors of the sides $AB$, $BC$, $CA$, respectively, of a given triangle $ABC$ so that $$\frac{|AK|}{|KB|}=\frac{|BL|}{|LC|}=\frac{|CM|}{|MA|}.$$ Prove that the triangles $ABC$ and $KLM$ have a common orthocentre if and only if the triangle $ABC$ is equilateral.

On a table there are $k$ heaps with $1, 2, \ldots, k$ stones, where $k\ge 3$. In the first step we choose any $3$ heaps on the table, merge them into one and remove $1$ stone from this new heap (off the table). In the second step we again merge some three heaps into one and then take $2$ stones away from it. In general, in the $i$-th step we merge any three heaps which together contain more than $i$ stones into one heap and then remove $i$ stones from it. Suppose that after several steps a single heap with $p$ stones remains on the table. Prove that the number $p$ is a perfect square if and only if both numbers $2k+2$ and $3k+1$ are perfect squares. Further, find the smallest $k$ for which the number $p$ is a perfect square.

Let $n$ be a given positive integer. Solve the system of equations $$\begin{aligned}x_1+x_2^2+x_3^3+\cdots+x_n^n&=n,\\ x_1+2x_2+3x_3+\cdots+nx_n&=\frac{n(n+1)}{2}\end{aligned}$$ with unknowns $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$ in the set of non-negative real numbers.

A convex quadrilateral $ABCD$ is inscribed in a circle with centre $O$ and circumscribed about a circle with centre $I$. Its diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ intersect at the point $P$. Prove that the points $O$, $I$ and $P$ lie on a line.
Determine all positive integers $n \ge 3$ for which the polynomial $$P(x)=x^n-3x^{n-1}+2x^{n-2}+6$$ can be expressed as a product of two polynomials of positive degree with integer coefficients.

Let us distribute $n \ge 1$ labelled balls among nine persons $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$, $E$, $F$, $G$, $H$, $I$. Determine in how many ways this can be done under the condition that the person $A$ receives the same number of balls as the persons $B$, $C$, $D$, $E$ together.

A convex quadrilateral $ABCD$ is given. Determine the set of all points $P$ lying inside the quadrilateral $ABCD$ for which $$S_{PAB}\cdot S_{PCD}=S_{PBC}\cdot S_{PDA},$$ where $S_{XYZ}$ denotes the area of the triangle $XYZ$.
Find all pairs of integers $(x,y)$ satisfying the equation $$y(x+y)=x^3-7x^2+11x-3.$$

Five distinct points $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$, $E$ lie in this order on a circle of radius $r$ and satisfy $|AC|=|BD|=|CE|=r$. Prove that the triangle whose vertices are the orthocentres of the triangles $ACD$, $BCD$ and $BCE$ is right-angled.

There are $n$ children sitting around a round table. Erika is the oldest of them and she has $n$ candies; the other children have no candies. Erika decided to distribute the candies and set the following rules. In every round, all children who have at least two candies raise their hands. Erika chooses one of them, and this child gives one candy to each of his or her two neighbours. (So in the first round only Erika raises her hand and gives one candy to each of her two neighbours.) Determine for which $n \ge 3$ the distribution can end after a finite number of rounds with every child having exactly one candy.
The sum of four real numbers is $9$ and the sum of their squares is $21$. Prove that these numbers can be denoted by $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$ so that the inequality $ab-cd \ge 2$ holds.

Prove that for every positive integer $k \ge 1$ there exists a positive integer $n$ such that the decimal representation of the number $2^n$ contains a block of exactly $k$ consecutive zeros, i.e. $$2^n=\ldots a\underbrace{00\ldots0}_{k\text{ zeros}}b\ldots,$$ where the digits $a$, $b$ are nonzero.
Determine how many sequences of integers $(a_n)_{n=1}^{\infty}$ exist such that for every positive integer $n$ $$a_n \ne -1 \quad\text{and}\quad a_{n+2}=\frac{a_n+2006}{a_{n+1}+1}.$$

Determine whether there exists a convex pentagon $A_1A_2A_3A_4A_5$ such that for each $i=1,2,3,4,5$ the lines $A_iA_{i+3}$ and $A_{i+1}A_{i+2}$ are not parallel and intersect at a point $B_i$, and the points $B_1$, $B_2$, $B_3$, $B_4$, $B_5$ lie on a line. (We set $A_6=A_1$, $A_7=A_2$ and $A_8=A_3$.)
Find all polynomials $P$ with real coefficients for which the equality $$P(x^2)=P(x)\cdot P(x+2)$$ holds for every real number $x$.

Let $a_1=a_2=1$ and $a_{k+2}=a_{k+1}+a_k$ for any $k\in\mathbb{N}$ (the Fibonacci sequence). Prove that for any natural number $m$ there exists an index $k$ such that the number $a_k^4-a_k-2$ is divisible by $m$.

Let $k$ be the circumcircle of a given convex quadrilateral $ABCD$ with the property that the half-lines $DA$ and $CB$ meet at a point $E$ for which $|CD|^2=|AD|\cdot|ED|$ holds. Let us denote by $F$ ($F\ne A$) the point of intersection of the circle $k$ with the perpendicular to $ED$ at $A$. Prove that the segments $AD$ and $CF$ are congruent if and only if the circumcenter of the triangle $ABE$ lies on $ED$.

For any real number $p\ge 1$ let us consider the set of all real numbers $x$ with $$p<x<\left(2+\sqrt{p+\frac{1}{4}}\right)^2.$$ Prove that from such a given set one can select four mutually different natural numbers $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$ with $ab=cd$.

Find for which $$n\in\{3\,900, 3\,901, 3\,902, 3\,903, 3\,904, 3\,905, 3\,906, 3\,907, 3\,908, 3\,909\}$$ the set $\{1,2,3,\ldots,n\}$ can be partitioned into (disjoint) triples in such a way that one of the three numbers in any triple is the sum of the other two.

Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral. A circle passing through the points $A$ and $D$ and a circle passing through the points $B$ and $C$ are externally tangent at a point $P$ inside the quadrilateral. Suppose that $$|\angle PAB|+|\angle PDC|\le 90^\circ \quad\text{and}\quad |\angle PBA|+|\angle PCD|\le 90^\circ.$$ Prove that $|AB|+|CD|\ge|BC|+|AD|$.
Determine all triples $(x,y,z)$ of positive numbers satisfying the system of equations $$\begin{aligned}2x^3&=2y(x^2+1)-(z^2+1),\\ 2y^4&=3z(y^2+1)-2(x^2+1),\\ 2z^5&=4x(z^2+1)-3(y^2+1).\end{aligned}$$
Given is a convex hexagon $ABCDEF$, such that $\angle A=\angle C=\angle E$ and $AB=BC$, $CD=DE$, $EF=FA$. Prove that the lines $AD$, $BE$ and $CF$ have a common point.
Determine all prime numbers $p$, such that the number $$\binom{p}{1}^2+\binom{p}{2}^2+\ldots+\binom{p}{p-1}^2$$ is divisible by $p^3$.
Prove that there exists a positive integer $n$, such that for all integers $k$ the number $k^2+k+n$ has no prime divisors less than $2008$.
Given is a regular pentagon $ABCDE$. Determine the least value of the expression $$\frac{PA+PB}{PC+PD+PE},$$ where $P$ is an arbitrary point lying in the plane of the pentagon $ABCDE$.

Find all triples $(k,m,n)$ of positive integers with the following property: The square with the side length $m$ can be cut into some number of rectangles of dimensions $1\times k$ and exactly one square of the side length $n$.

Let $\mathbb{R}^+$ denote the set of all positive real numbers. Find all functions $f\colon \mathbb{R}^+\to\mathbb{R}^+$ which for arbitrary $x,y\in\mathbb{R}^+$ satisfy the condition $$\bigl(1+yf(x)\bigr)\bigl(1-yf(x+y)\bigr)=1.$$

For given positive integers $a$, $k$, the sequence $(a_n)_{n=1}^{\infty}$ is defined by $$a_1=a \quad\text{and}\quad a_{n+1}=a_n+k\cdot\varrho(a_n) \quad\text{for } n=1,2,\ldots,$$ where $\varrho(m)$ denotes the product of the digits of the number $m$ written in the decimal system (for example $\varrho(413)=12$, $\varrho(308)=0$, etc.). Prove that there exist positive integers $a$, $k$ such that the sequence $(a_n)_{n=1}^{\infty}$ contains exactly $2009$ distinct numbers.

Let $k$ be the excircle of a given triangle $ABC$ tangent to the side $BC$. Choose a line $p$ parallel to the side $BC$ that intersects the segments $AB$, $AC$ at points $D$, $E$. Denote by $l$ the incircle of the triangle $ADE$. The tangents to the circle $k$ drawn from the points $D$, $E$ and not passing through the point $A$ intersect at a point $P$. The tangents to the circle $l$ drawn from the points $B$, $C$ and not passing through the point $A$ intersect at a point $Q$. Prove that the line $PQ$ passes through a fixed point independent of the choice of the line $p$.

A circle $k$ and its chord $AB$, which is not a diameter, are given. A point $C$ is chosen arbitrarily in the interior of the longer arc $AB$ of the circle $k$. The images of the points $A$ and $B$ under the reflections in the lines $BC$ and $AC$ are denoted by $K$ and $L$, respectively. Prove that the distance between the midpoints of the segments $KL$ and $AB$ does not depend on the position of the point $C$.

An $n$-tuple of integers $a_1,\ldots,a_n$ satisfying the following conditions is given:

(i) $1\le a_1<a_2<\cdots<a_n\le 50$;

(ii) for every $n$-tuple of positive integers $b_1,\ldots,b_n$ there exist a positive integer $m$ and an $n$-tuple of positive integers $c_1,\ldots,c_n$ such that $$m\cdot b_i=c_i^{a_i} \quad\text{for } i=1,\ldots,n.$$

Prove that $n\le 16$ and determine the number of distinct $n$-tuples $a_1,\ldots,a_n$ satisfying the given conditions for $n=16$.

Let $n\ge 16$ be a positive integer. Consider the set $$G=\bigl\{(x,y) : x,y\in\{1,2,\ldots,n\}\bigr\}$$ consisting of $n^2$ points of the plane. Let $A$ be an arbitrary subset of the set $G$ containing at least $4n\sqrt{n}$ elements. Prove that there exist at least $n^2$ convex quadrilaterals with vertices in $A$ all of whose diagonals pass through one point.
Determine all triples $(a,b,c)$ of positive real numbers which are solutions of the system of equations $$\begin{aligned}a\sqrt{b}-c&=a,\\ b\sqrt{c}-a&=b,\\ c\sqrt{a}-b&=c.\end{aligned}$$
Consider arbitrary $60$ points in a disc of radius $1$. Prove that there exists a point on the boundary of the disc such that the sum of its distances from all $60$ points is not greater than $80$.

Let $p$ be a prime. Prove that one can choose $p^3$ squares of a $p^2\times p^2$ chessboard in such a way that the centres of no four chosen squares are the vertices of a rectangle with sides parallel to the edges of the chessboard.

Find the largest integer $k$ for which the following statement is true: Arbitrary $2010$ non-degenerate triangles are given. In each triangle the sides are coloured so that one is blue, one is red and one is white. For each colour separately we order the lengths of the sides. We obtain $$\begin{aligned}&b_1\le b_2\le\ldots\le b_{2010} &&\text{for the lengths of the blue sides,}\\ &r_1\le r_2\le\ldots\le r_{2010} &&\text{for the lengths of the red sides,}\\ &w_1\le w_2\le\ldots\le w_{2010} &&\text{for the lengths of the white sides.}\end{aligned}$$ Then there exist at least $k$ indices $j$ such that a non-degenerate triangle with side lengths $b_j$, $r_j$, $w_j$ can be formed.
Positive real numbers $x$, $y$, $z$ satisfy $x+y+z\ge 6$. Find the smallest possible value of the expression $$x^2+y^2+z^2+\frac{x}{y^2+z+1}+\frac{y}{z^2+x+1}+\frac{z}{x^2+y+1}.$$
Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral such that $$|AB|+|CD|=\sqrt{2}\cdot|AC| \quad\text{and}\quad |BC|+|DA|=\sqrt{2}\cdot|BD|.$$ Prove that $ABCD$ is a parallelogram.
Let $a$, $b$, $c$ be positive real numbers such that $a^2<bc$. Prove that $b^3+ac^2>ab(a+c)$.

There are $n$ non-negative integers written on a blackboard whose greatest common divisor is $1$. In one step we may erase two numbers $x$, $y$ such that $x\ge y$ and replace them by the pair of numbers $x-y$, $2y$. Determine for which $n$-tuples of initial numbers we can reach a state in which $n-1$ of the numbers on the blackboard are zeros.

Points $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$ lie in this order on a circle, where $AB\nparallel CD$ and the length of the arc $AB$ containing the points $C$, $D$ is twice the length of the arc $CD$ not containing the points $A$, $B$. Let $E$ be the point in the half-plane $ABC$ such that $|AC|=|AE|$ and $|BD|=|BE|$. Prove that if the perpendicular from the point $E$ to the line $AB$ passes through the midpoint of the arc $CD$ not containing the points $A$, $B$, then $|\angle ACB|=108^\circ$.

A polynomial $P(x)$ with integer coefficients satisfies the following condition: If polynomials $F(x)$, $G(x)$, $Q(x)$ with integer coefficients satisfy $$P(Q(x))=F(x)\cdot G(x),$$ then at least one of the polynomials $F(x)$, $G(x)$ is constant. Prove that $P(x)$ is a constant polynomial.

In a convex quadrilateral $ABCD$, let $M$, $N$ be the midpoints of the sides $AD$, $BC$, respectively. Points $K$ and $L$ are chosen on the sides $AB$ and $CD$, respectively, such that $|\angle MKA|=|\angle NLC|$. Prove that if the lines $BD$, $KM$, $LN$ pass through one point, then $$|\angle KMN|=|\angle BDC| \quad\text{and}\quad |\angle LNM|=|\angle ABD|.$$
Let $a$ be an arbitrary integer. Prove that there exist infinitely many primes $p$ such that $$p\mid n^2+3 \quad\text{and}\quad p\mid m^3-a$$ for some integers $n$, $m$.

For a given positive integer $n$, let $\tau(n)$ denote the number of positive divisors of $n$ and $\varphi(n)$ the number of positive integers not greater than $n$ that are coprime to $n$. Find all $n$ for which one of the three numbers $n$, $\tau(n)$, $\varphi(n)$ is the arithmetic mean of the other two.
Find all functions $f\colon\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ such that the equality $$f(x+f(y))-f(x)=(x+f(y))^4-x^4$$ holds for all $x,y\in\mathbb{R}$.

A cyclic quadrilateral $ABCD$ with circumcircle $\omega$ is given. Let $I$, $J$, $K$ be the incentres of the triangles $ABC$, $ACD$, $ABD$, respectively. Let $E$ be the midpoint of the arc $DB$ of the circle $\omega$ containing the point $A$. The line $EK$ intersects the circle $\omega$ at a point $F$ ($F\ne E$). Prove that the points $C$, $F$, $I$, $J$ lie on a circle.

A right triangle $ABC$ with hypotenuse $AB$ is given, and a point $P$ lies in the interior of the shorter arc $AC$ of the circumcircle of the triangle $ABC$. The line through the point $C$ perpendicular to the line $CP$ intersects the lines $AP$, $BP$ at points $K$, $L$, respectively. Prove that the ratio of the areas of the triangles $BKL$ and $ACP$ does not depend on the position of the point $P$.

The city of Mar del Plata has the shape of a square $WSEN$ and is divided by $2(n+1)$ streets into $n\times n$ blocks, where $n$ is a given even number (streets also run along the perimeter of the square). Each block measures $100\times 100$ metres. All streets in Mar del Plata are one-way, each street has the same direction along its whole length, and adjacent parallel streets always have opposite directions. The street $WS$ is driven in the direction from $W$ to $S$ and the street $WN$ from $W$ to $N$. A street-watering car starts at the point $W$. It wants to get to the point $E$ and water as many streets as possible on the way. What is the length of the longest route it can travel if it does not want to traverse any $100$-metre segment more than once? (The figure shows, for $n=6$, the plan of the city and one of the possible, but not longest, routes of the watering car.)

Positive real numbers $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$ satisfy the conditions $$abcd=4,\qquad a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2=10.$$ Determine the largest possible value of the expression $ab+bc+cd+da$.

A cyclic quadrilateral $ABCD$ with $|BC|=|CD|$ is given. Let $\omega$ be the circle with centre $C$ tangent to the diagonal $BD$, and let $I$ be the incentre of the triangle $ABD$. Prove that the line through the point $I$ parallel to $AB$ is tangent to the circle $\omega$.
Prove that for every real number $x>0$ and every integer $n>0$ $$x^n+\frac{1}{x^n}-2\ge n^2\left(x+\frac{1}{x}-2\right).$$

For every rational number $r$ consider the statement: If $x$ is a real number such that the numbers $x^2-rx$ and $x^3-rx$ are both rational, then $x$ is also rational.

a) Prove the statement for $r\ge\frac{4}{3}$ and for $r\le 0$.

b) Let $p$, $q$ be distinct odd primes such that $3p<4q$. Prove that the statement does not hold for $r=\frac{p}{q}$.
Let $a$, $b$ be integers, where $b$ is not the square of an integer. Prove that $x^2+ax+b$ can be the square of an integer for only finitely many integer values of $x$.

A triangular grid divides an equilateral triangle with side length $n$ into $n^2$ triangular cells (see the figure). Some cells are infected. A cell that is not yet infected becomes infected if it shares a side with at least two already infected cells. For $n=12$, determine the smallest possible number of initially infected cells for which it is possible that after some time all cells of the original triangle are infected.

A triangle $ABC$ and its circumcircle are given. The point $P$ is the midpoint of the arc $BAC$. The circle with diameter $CP$ intersects the bisector of the angle $BAC$ at points $K$, $L$ ($|AK|<|AL|$). The point $M$ is the reflection of the point $L$ in the line $BC$. Prove that the circumcircle of the triangle $BKM$ passes through the midpoint of the segment $BC$.

Prove that positive real numbers $a$, $b$, $c$ satisfy the equation $$a^4+b^4+c^4+4a^2b^2c^2=2\left(a^2b^2+a^2c^2+b^2c^2\right)$$ if and only if there exists a triangle $ABC$ with interior angles $\alpha$, $\beta$, $\gamma$ such that $\sin\alpha=a$, $\sin\beta=b$ and $\sin\gamma=c$.

For given positive integers $a$, $b$, $x_1$ we construct the sequence of numbers $(x_n)_{n=1}^{\infty}$ satisfying the relation $x_n=ax_{n-1}+b$ for every $n\ge 2$. Determine a condition on the given numbers $a$, $b$ and $x_1$ which is necessary and sufficient for the implication $m\mid n \Rightarrow x_m\mid x_n$ to hold for all indices $m$, $n$.

A convex quadrilateral $ABCD$ with $|\angle ABC|=|\angle ADC|=135^\circ$ is given. Points $M$, $N$ are chosen on the half-lines $AB$, $AD$, respectively, such that $|\angle MCD|=|\angle NCB|=90^\circ$. The circumcircles of the triangles $AMN$ and $ABD$ intersect for the second time at a point $K\ne A$. Prove that the lines $AK$ and $KC$ are perpendicular.

A triangle $ABC$ is given, and $P$ is the midpoint of the side $AC$. A circle $k$ intersects the segments $AP$, $CP$, $BC$, $AB$ at their interior points $K$, $L$, $M$, $N$, respectively. Let $S$ be the midpoint of $KL$. Suppose that $$2\cdot|AN|\cdot|AB|\cdot|CL|=2\cdot|CM|\cdot|BC|\cdot|AK|=|AC|\cdot|AK|\cdot|CL|.$$ Prove that if $P\ne S$, then the intersection of the lines $KN$ and $ML$ lies on the perpendicular bisector of the segment $PS$.

Determine all positive integers $n$ satisfying the following condition: for all non-negative integers $k$, $m$ such that $k+m\le n$, the numbers $\binom{n-k}{m}$ and $\binom{n-m}{k}$ leave the same remainder upon division by two.

Let $n\ge 6$ be an integer and let $\mathcal{F}$ be a system of $3$-element subsets of the set $\{1,2,\ldots,n\}$ satisfying the following condition: for all $1\le i<j\le n$ there exist at least $\left\lfloor\frac{1}{3}n\right\rfloor-1$ subsets $A\in\mathcal{F}$ such that $i,j\in A$. Prove that for some integer $m\ge 1$ there exist mutually disjoint subsets $A_1,A_2,\ldots,A_m\in\mathcal{F}$ such that $$|A_1\cup A_2\cup\ldots\cup A_m|\ge n-5.$$

Pairwise distinct points $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$ and $E$ lie in this order on a circle of radius $r$, where $AB=CD=DE>r$. Prove that the triangle whose vertices are the centroids of the triangles $ABD$, $BCD$ and $ADE$ is obtuse.

A family of sets $\mathcal{F}$ is called perfect if the following condition holds: for every triple of sets $X_1, X_2, X_3\in\mathcal{F}$, at least one of the sets $$(X_1\setminus X_2)\cap X_3,\qquad (X_2\setminus X_1)\cap X_3$$ is empty. Prove that if $\mathcal{F}$ is a perfect family consisting of subsets of some finite set $U$, then $|\mathcal{F}|\le|U|+1$.

Real numbers $x$, $y$, $z$ satisfy the equation $$\frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{y}+\frac{1}{z}+x+y+z=0$$ and none of them lies in the open interval $(-1,1)$. Find the largest possible value of the expression $x+y+z$.

A strange calculator has only two buttons, and on each of them some positive two-digit number is written. At the beginning the display of the calculator shows the number $1$. After the button with the number $N$ is pressed, the calculator replaces the currently displayed number $X$ by the number $X\cdot N$ or $X+N$, where multiplication and addition are used alternately (multiplication first). For example, if the number $10$ is on the first button and the number $20$ on the second, then successive presses of the first, the second, the first and once more the first button make the calculator display successively the numbers $1\cdot 10=10$, $10+20=30$, $30\cdot 10=300$ and $300+10=310$. Decide whether there exist values of the two-digit numbers on the buttons of the calculator for which infinitely many numbers ending in

(a) $2015$,

(b) $5813$

can be shown on the display.

Triangle $ABC$ is acute but not equilateral. Let $O$ and $H$ be its circumcentre and orthocentre, respectively. A circle $k$ passes through the point $B$ and is tangent to the line $AC$ at the point $A$. A circle $l$ has its centre on the ray $BH$ and is tangent to the line $AB$ at the point $A$. The circles $k$ and $l$ intersect at a point $X$ different from $A$. Prove that $\angle HXO=180^\circ-\angle BAC$.

Let $n$ be an even positive integer. There are $n$ real numbers written on a blackboard. In one move we may choose two numbers, erase them and replace each of them by their product. Prove that for every initial $n$-tuple of numbers it is possible to obtain $n$ equal numbers on the blackboard after a finite number of moves.

Let $\mathcal{P}$ be an $n$-gon, where $n>4$. Prove that there exist three distinct vertices $A$, $B$, $C$ of it with the following property: if $l_1$, $l_2$, $l_3$ are the lengths of the three polygonal lines into which the vertices $A$, $B$, $C$ divide the perimeter of the polygon $\mathcal{P}$, then there exists a triangle with side lengths $l_1$, $l_2$, $l_3$.

Let $m,n>2$ be given even numbers. Consider an $m\times n$ table each of whose cells is coloured either black or white. Guessing Hanka does not see the colouring, but she may ask a soothsayer certain questions. More precisely, she may ask about two adjacent cells (sharing a common side), and the soothsayer reveals whether these two cells have the same colour or different colours. Hanka's task is to determine the parity of the number of pairs of adjacent cells that have different colours. What is the minimum number of questions that certainly suffices for Hanka to be able to determine the correct answer?

Let $n$ be a given positive integer. For a finite set $M$ of positive integers and for every $i\in\{0,1,\ldots,n-1\}$, denote by $s_i$ the number of nonempty subsets of $M$ whose sum of elements leaves remainder $i$ upon division by $n$. We say that the set $M$ is $n$-balanced if $s_0=s_1=\ldots=s_{n-1}$. For example, for $n=5$ and $M=\{1,3,4\}$ we have $s_0=s_1=s_2=1$ and $s_3=s_4=2$, so $M$ is not $5$-balanced. Prove that for every odd positive integer $n$ there exists an $n$-balanced subset of the set $\{1,2,\ldots,n\}$.

Find all quadruples $(a,b,c,d)$ of real numbers that are solutions of the system $$\begin{aligned}(a+b)(a^2+b^2)&=(c+d)(c^2+d^2),\\(a+c)(a^2+c^2)&=(b+d)(b^2+d^2),\\(a+d)(a^2+d^2)&=(b+c)(b^2+c^2).\end{aligned}$$
Prove that for every nonnegative integer $n$ there exist integers $x$, $y$, $z$ such that $$\gcd(x,y,z)=1 \quad\text{and}\quad x^2+y^2+z^2=3^{2^n}.$$

An acute triangle $ABC$ with $AB<AC$ is given. Let $\Omega$ be its circumcircle. The tangent to $\Omega$ at $A$ meets the line $BC$ at $D$. Let $G$ be the centroid of triangle $ABC$, and let the line $AG$ meet $\Omega$ at $H\ne A$. Suppose that the line $DG$ meets the lines $AB$ and $AC$ at $E$ and $F$, respectively. Prove that $\angle EHG=\angle GHF$.

Find all positive real numbers $c$ with the following property: there exist infinitely many pairs of positive integers $(n,m)$ such that $n\ge m+c\sqrt{m-1}+1$ and among the numbers $n,n+1,\ldots,2n-m$ there is no square of an integer.

An acute triangle $ABC$ with circumcircle $\omega$ is given. A point $D$ is given on the arc $BC$ of $\omega$ not containing the point $A$. A point $E$ lies inside triangle $ABC$, not on the line $AD$, and satisfies $\angle DBE=\angle ACB$ and $\angle DCE=\angle ABC$. Consider the point $F$ on the line $AD$ such that $EF\parallel BC$, and the point $G\ne A$ on the circle $\omega$ such that $AF=FG$. Prove that the points $D$, $E$, $F$, $G$ lie on one circle.

Let $k$ be a positive integer. A finite sequence of integers $x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n$ is written on the board. Maťko and Kubko play a game which proceeds in the following rounds:

• In each round, Maťko first divides the sequence currently on the board into two or more contiguous subsequences (that is, each subsequence consists of consecutive terms of the original sequence). Here, if the number of subsequences is greater than $2$, the sum of the numbers in each of them must be a multiple of $k$.

• Then Kubko chooses one of the subsequences and erases all the other subsequences from the board.

The game ends at the moment when only one number remains written on the board. Prove that Maťko can choose his moves so that, regardless of Kubko's moves, the game ends after at most $3k$ rounds.

A triangle $ABC$ is given. A line $l$ is parallel to the side $BC$ and meets the sides $AB$, $AC$ at points $D$, $E$, respectively, and the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ at points $F$, $G$, so that the points $F$, $D$, $E$, $G$ lie on the line $l$ in this order. The circumcircles of triangles $FEB$ and $DCG$ meet at points $P$ and $Q$. Prove that the points $A$, $P$, $Q$ lie on one line.

Each of the $4n^2$ cells of a $2n\times 2n$ table ($n\ge 1$) is coloured either red or blue. We say that a set of four mutually distinct cells of the table is nice if these cells can be labelled $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$ so that $A$ and $B$ lie in the same row, $C$ and $D$ lie in the same row, $A$ and $C$ lie in the same column, $B$ and $D$ lie in the same column, the cells $A$ and $D$ are blue and the cells $B$ and $C$ are red. Determine the largest possible number of nice sets in such a table.
Find all functions $f\colon(0,+\infty)\to\mathbb{R}$ such that $$f(x)-f(x+y)=f\left(\frac{x}{y}\right)f(x+y)\qquad\text{for all } x,y>0.$$
Determine all functions $f\colon\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ such that, for all real numbers $x$ and $y$, $$f(x^2+xy)=f(x)f(y)+yf(x)+xf(x+y).$$

Let $ABC$ be an acute scalene triangle. Let $D$ and $E$ be points on the sides $AB$ and $AC$, respectively, such that $BD=CE$. Denote by $O_1$ and $O_2$ the circumcentres of the triangles $ABE$ and $ACD$, respectively. Prove that the circumcircles of the triangles $ABC$, $ADE$ and $AO_1O_2$ have a common point different from $A$.

There are $2018$ players sitting around a round table. At the beginning of the game we arbitrarily deal all the cards from a deck of $K$ cards to the players (some players may receive no cards). In each turn we choose a player who draws one card from each of the two neighbours. It is only allowed to choose a player whose each neighbour holds a nonzero number of cards. The game terminates when there is no such player. Determine the largest possible value of $K$ such that, no matter how we deal the cards and how we choose the players, the game always terminates after a finite number of turns.

Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with the perimeter of $2s$. We are given three disjoint circles with disjoint interiors with the centres $A$, $B$ and $C$, respectively. Prove that there exists a circle with the radius of $s$ which contains all the three circles.

In a rectangle with dimensions $2\times 3$ there is a polyline of length $36$. Show that there exists a line parallel to two sides of the rectangle, which intersects the other two sides in their interior points and intersects the polyline in fewer than $10$ points.

We say that a positive integer $n$ is fantastic, if there exist positive rational numbers $a$ and $b$ such that $$n=a+\frac{1}{a}+b+\frac{1}{b}.$$

(a) Prove that there exist infinitely many prime numbers $p$ such that no multiple of $p$ is fantastic.

(b) Prove that there exist infinitely many prime numbers $p$ such that some multiple of $p$ is fantastic.

Let $\omega$ be a circle. Points $A$, $B$, $C$, $X$, $D$, $Y$ lie on $\omega$ in this order such that $BD$ is its diameter and $DX=DY=DP$, where $P$ is the intersection of $AC$ and $BD$. Denote by $E$, $F$ the intersections of line $XP$ with lines $AB$, $BC$, respectively. Prove that points $B$, $E$, $F$, $Y$ lie on a single circle.

We consider positive integers $n$ having at least six positive divisors. Let the positive divisors of $n$ be arranged in a sequence $(d_i)_{1\le i\le k}$ with $$1=d_1<d_2<\cdots<d_k=n\quad(k\ge 6).$$ Find all positive integers $n$ such that $$n=d_5^2+d_6^2.$$

A dissection of a convex polygon into finitely many triangles by segments is called a trilateration if no three vertices of the created triangles lie on a single line (vertices of some triangles might lie inside the polygon). We say that a trilateration is good if its segments can be replaced with one-way arrows in such a way that the arrows along every triangle of the trilateration form a cycle and the arrows along the whole convex polygon also form a cycle. Find all $n\ge 3$ such that the regular $n$-gon has a good trilateration.
Let $\alpha$ be a given real number. Determine all pairs $(f,g)$ of functions $f,g\colon\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ satisfying $$xf(x+y)+\alpha\cdot yf(x-y)=g(x)+g(y)$$ for all $x,y\in\mathbb{R}$.

Determine whether there exist $100$ disks $D_2,D_3,\ldots,D_{101}$ in the plane such that the following conditions hold for all pairs $(a,b)$ of indices satisfying $2\le a<b\le 101$:

1. If $a\mid b$ then $D_a$ is contained in $D_b$.

2. If $\gcd(a,b)=1$ then $D_a$ and $D_b$ are disjoint.

(A disk $D(O,r)$ is a set of points in the plane whose distance to a given point $O$ is at most a given positive real number $r$.)

Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with $AB<AC$ and $\angle BAC=60^\circ$. Denote its altitudes by $AD$, $BE$, $CF$ and its orthocenter by $H$. Let $K$, $L$, $M$ be the midpoints of sides $BC$, $CA$, $AB$, respectively. Prove that the midpoints of segments $AH$, $DK$, $EL$, $FM$ lie on a single circle.

Let $ABCD$ be a parallelogram whose diagonals meet at $P$. Denote by $M$ the midpoint of $AB$. Let $Q$ be a point such that $QA$ is tangent to the circumcircle of $MAD$ and $QB$ is tangent to the circumcircle of $MBC$. Prove that points $Q$, $M$, $P$ are collinear.

Given a positive integer $n$, we say that a real number $x$ is $n$-good if there exist $n$ positive integers $a_1,\ldots,a_n$ such that $$x=\frac{1}{a_1}+\cdots+\frac{1}{a_n}.$$ Find all positive integers $k$ for which the following assertion is true:

if $a,b$ are real numbers such that the closed interval $[a,b]$ contains infinitely many $2020$-good numbers, then the interval $[a,b]$ contains at least one $k$-good number.

The numbers $1,2,\ldots,2020$ are written on the blackboard. Venus and Serena play the following game. First, Venus connects by a line segment two numbers such that one of them divides the other. Then Serena connects by a line segment two numbers which has not been connected and such that one of them divides the other. Then Venus again and they continue until there is a triangle with one vertex in $2020$, i.e. $2020$ is connected to two numbers that are connected with each other. The girl that has drawn the last line segment (completed the triangle) is the winner. Which of the girls has a winning strategy?
Let $a$ be a given real number. Find all functions $f\colon\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ such that $$(x+y)(f(x)-f(y))=a(x-y)f(x+y)$$ holds for all $x,y\in\mathbb{R}$.

Let $n$ be a positive integer and let $d(n)$ denote the number of ordered pairs of positive integers $(x,y)$ such that $$(x+1)^2-xy(2x-xy+2y)+(y+1)^2=n.$$ Find the smallest positive integer $n$ satisfying $d(n)=61$.

Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle. Let $P$ be a point such that $PB$ and $PC$ are tangent to circumcircle of $ABC$. Let $X$ and $Y$ be variable points on $AB$ and $AC$, respectively, such that $\angle XPY=2\angle BAC$ and $P$ lies in the interior of triangle $AXY$. Let $Z$ be the reflection of $A$ across $XY$. Prove that the circumcircle of $XYZ$ passes through a fixed point.
Find all quadruples $(a,b,c,d)$ of positive integers satisfying $\gcd(a,b,c,d)=1$ and $$a\mid b+c,\quad b\mid c+d,\quad c\mid d+a,\quad d\mid a+b.$$

In an acute triangle $ABC$, the incircle $\omega$ touches $BC$ at $D$. Let $I_a$ be the excenter of $ABC$ opposite to $A$, and let $M$ be the midpoint of $DI_a$. Prove that the circumcircle of triangle $BMC$ is tangent to $\omega$.

For any two convex polygons $P_1$ and $P_2$ with mutually distinct vertices, denote by $f(P_1,P_2)$ the total number of their vertices that lie on a side of the other polygon. For each positive integer $n\ge 4$, determine $$\max\{f(P_1,P_2)\mid P_1 \text{ and } P_2 \text{ are convex } n\text{-gons}\}.$$

(We say that a polygon is convex if all its internal angles are strictly less than $180^\circ$.)
Determine the number of $2021$-tuples of positive integers such that the number $3$ is an element of the tuple and consecutive elements of the tuple differ by at most $1$.

The sequence $a_1,a_2,a_3,\ldots$ satisfies $a_1=1$, and for all $n\ge 2$, it holds that $$a_n=\begin{cases}a_{n-1}+3 & \text{if } n-1\in\{a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_{n-1}\};\\ a_{n-1}+2 & \text{otherwise.}\end{cases}$$ Prove that for all positive integers $n$, we have $$a_n<n\cdot\left(1+\sqrt{2}\right).$$

Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle and suppose points $A$, $A_b$, $B_a$, $B$, $B_c$, $C_b$, $C$, $C_a$, and $A_c$ lie on its perimeter in this order. Let $A_1
e A$ be the second intersection point of the circumcircles of triangles $AA_bC_a$ and $AA_cB_a$. Analogously, $B_1
e B$ is the second intersection point of the circumcircles of triangles $BB_cA_b$ and $BB_aC_b$, and $C_1
e C$ is the second intersection point of the circumcircles of triangles $CC_aB_c$ and $CC_bA_c$. Suppose that the points $A_1$, $B_1$, and $C_1$ are all distinct, lie inside the triangle $ABC$, and do not lie on a single line. Prove that lines $AA_1$, $BB_1$, $CC_1$, and the circumcircle of triangle $A_1B_1C_1$ all pass through a common point.

Let $k\le 2022$ be a positive integer. Alice and Bob play a game on a $2022\times 2022$ board. Initially, all cells are white. Alice starts and the players alternate. In her turn, Alice can either color one white cell in red or pass her turn. In his turn, Bob can either color a $k\times k$ square of white cells in blue or pass his turn. Once both players pass, the game ends and the person who colored more cells wins (a draw can occur).

For each $1\le k\le 2022$, determine which player (if any) has a winning strategy.
Find all functions $f\colon(0,\infty)\to(0,\infty)$ such that $$f\left(f(x)+\frac{y+1}{f(y)}\right)=\frac{1}{f(y)}+x+1$$ for all $x,y>0$.

Circles $\Omega_1$ and $\Omega_2$ with different radii intersect at two points, denote one of them by $P$. A variable line $\ell$ passing through $P$ intersects the arc of $\Omega_1$ which is outside of $\Omega_2$ at $X_1$, and the arc of $\Omega_2$ which is outside of $\Omega_1$ at $X_2$. Let $R$ be the point on segment $X_1X_2$ such that $X_1P=RX_2$. The tangent to $\Omega_1$ through $X_1$ meets the tangent to $\Omega_2$ through $X_2$ at $T$. Prove that line $RT$ is tangent to a fixed circle, independent of the choice of $\ell$.

Given a positive integer $n$, denote by $\tau(n)$ the number of positive divisors of $n$, and by $\sigma(n)$ the sum of all positive divisors of $n$. Find all positive integers $n$ satisfying $$\sigma(n)=\tau(n)\cdot\left\lceil\sqrt{n}\right\rceil.$$ (Here, $\lceil x\rceil$ denotes the smallest integer not less than $x$.)

Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $AB<AC$ and circumcenter $O$. The angle bisector of $\angle BAC$ meets the side $BC$ at $D$. The line through $D$ perpendicular to $BC$ meets the segment $AO$ at $X$. Furthermore, let $Y$ be the midpoint of segment $AD$. Prove that points $B$, $C$, $X$, $Y$ are concyclic.

Consider $26$ letters $A,\ldots,Z$. A string is a finite sequence consisting of those letters. We say that a string $s$ is nice if it contains each of the $26$ letters at least once, and each permutation of letters $A,\ldots,Z$ occurs in $s$ as a subsequence the same number of times. Prove that:

(a) There exists a nice string.

(b) Any nice string contains at least $2022$ letters.

(Here, a permutation $\pi$ of the $26$ letters is a subsequence of a string $s$ if there exist $26$ indices $i_1<i_2<\cdots<i_{26}$ such that $\pi=s_{i_1}s_{i_2}\ldots s_{i_{26}}$.)

Given an integer $n\ge 3$, determine the smallest positive number $k$ such that any two points in any $n$-gon (or at its boundary) in the plane can be connected by a polygonal path consisting of $k$ line segments contained in the $n$-gon (including its boundary).

Let $a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_n$ be real numbers so that for every $k=1,2,\ldots,n$ the following inequality holds: $$n\cdot a_k\ge\sum_{i=1}^{k}a_i^2.$$ Prove that there exist at least $\frac{n}{10}$ indices $k$ so that $a_k\le 1000$.

Given is a convex quadrilateral $ABCD$ with $\angle BAD=\angle BCD$ and $\angle ABC<\angle ADC$. Point $M$ is the midpoint of segment $AC$. Prove that there exist points $X$ and $Y$ on the segments $AB$ and $BC$, respectively, such that $XY\perp BD$, $MX=MY$ and $\angle XMY=\angle ADC-\angle ABC$.

Let $p$, $q$ and $r$ be positive real numbers such that the equation $$\lfloor pn\rfloor+\lfloor qn\rfloor+\lfloor rn\rfloor=n$$ is satisfied for infinitely many positive integers $n$.

(a) Prove that $p$, $q$ and $r$ are rational.

(b) Determine the number of positive integers $c$ such that there exist positive integers $a$ and $b$, for which the equation $$\left\lfloor\frac{n}{a}\right\rfloor+\left\lfloor\frac{n}{b}\right\rfloor+\left\lfloor\frac{cn}{202}\right\rfloor=n$$ is satisfied for infinitely many positive integers $n$.

Let $ABC$ be an acute-angled triangle with orthocenter $H$. Let $D$ be the foot of the altitude from $A$ to the line $BC$. Let $T$ be a point on the circle with diameter $AH$ such that this circle is internally tangent to the circumcircle of triangle $BDT$. Let $N$ be the midpoint of segment $AH$. Prove that $BT\perp CN$.

Given is an integer $n\ge 1$ and an $n\times n$ board, whose all cells are initially white. Peter the painter walks around the board and recolors the visited cells according to the following rules. Each walk of Peter starts at the bottom-left corner of the board and continues as follows:

• if he is standing on a white cell, he paints it black and moves one cell up (or walks off the board if he is in the top row);

• if he is standing on a black cell, he paints it white and moves one cell to the right (or walks off the board if he is in the rightmost column).

Peter's walk ends once he walks off the board. Determine the minimum positive integer $s$ with the following property: after exactly $s$ walks all the cells of the board will become white again.

E.g. for $n=3$ the states of the board after each of the initial five walks will be:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/cps_2023_p6_fig.png

Determine whether there exist $2024$ distinct positive integers satisfying the following: If we consider every possible ratio between two distinct numbers (we include both $a/b$ and $b/a$), we will obtain numbers with finite decimal expansions (after the decimal point) of mutually distinct non-zero lengths.

Example: The number $3.14159$ has decimal expansion $.14159$ of length $5$.

For a positive integer $n$, an $n$-configuration is a family of sets $\langle A_{i,j}\rangle_{1\le i,j\le n}$. An $n$-configuration is called sweet if for every pair of indices $(i,j)$ with $1\le i\le n-1$ and $1\le j\le n$ we have $A_{i,j}\subseteq A_{i+1,j}$ and $A_{j,i}\subseteq A_{j,i+1}$. Let $f(n,k)$ denote the number of sweet $n$-configurations such that $A_{n,n}\subseteq\{1,2,\ldots,k\}$. Determine which number is larger: $f(2024,2024^2)$ or $f(2024^2,2024)$.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle and $D$ a point on its side $BC$. Points $E$, $F$ lie on the lines $AB$, $AC$, respectively, such that $B$ lies between $A$ and $E$ and $BE=BD$ and $C$ lies between $A$ and $F$ and $CF=CD$. Let $P$ be a point such that $D$ is the incenter of triangle $PEF$. Prove that $P$ lies inside the circumcircle $\Omega$ of triangle $ABC$ or on it.

Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral, such that $AB=BC=CD$. There are points $X$, $Y$ on rays $CA$, $BD$, respectively, such that $BX=CY$. Let $P$, $Q$, $R$, $S$ be the midpoints of segments $BX$, $CY$, $XD$, $YA$, respectively. Prove that points $P$, $Q$, $R$, $S$ lie on a circle.
Let $\alpha\ne 0$ be a real number. Determine all functions $f\colon\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ such that $$f(x^2+y^2)=f(x-y)f(x+y)+\alpha yf(y)$$ holds for all $x,y\in\mathbb{R}$.

Determine whether there exist infinitely many triples $(a,b,c)$ of positive integers such that $p$ divides $\left\lfloor\left(a+b\sqrt{2024}\right)^p\right\rfloor-c$ for every prime $p$.

Note: $\lfloor x\rfloor$ denotes the largest integer not larger than $x$.
Let $a,b,c,d$ be nonnegative real numbers for which $a^2+b^2=ac+bd$ holds and $c,d$ are not both zero. Find maximum and minimum value of the expression $$\frac{ad+bc-cd}{c^2+d^2}.$$

Let $\{a_n\}_{n=1}^{\infty}$ be a sequence of positive integers such that for every positive integer $n$ $$a_{n+1}=(n+1)(a_n-n+1).$$ In terms of $a_1$, determine the greatest positive integer $k$ such that $\gcd(a_i,a_{i+1})=k$ for some positive integer $i\ge 2$. (Note that $\gcd(x,y)$ denotes the greatest common divisor of integers $x$ and $y$.)

Maryam and Artur play a game on a board, taking turns. At the beginning, the polynomial $XY-1$ is written on the board. Artur is the first to make a move. In each move, the player replaces the polynomial $P(X,Y)$ on the board with one of the following polynomials of their choice:

(a) $X\cdot P(X,Y)$

(b) $Y\cdot P(X,Y)$

(c) $P(X,Y)+a$, where $a\in(-\infty,2025]$ is an arbitrary integer.

The game stops after each player has made $2025$ moves. Let $Q(X,Y)$ be the polynomial on the board after the game ends. Maryam wins if the equation $Q(x,y)=0$ has a finite and odd number of positive integer solutions $(x,y)$. Prove that Maryam can always win the game, no matter how Artur plays.

The plane was divided by vertical and horizontal lines into unit squares. Determine whether it is possible to write integers into cells of this infinite grid so that:

(i) every cell contains exactly one integer

(ii) every integer appears exactly once

(iii) for every two cells $A$ and $B$ sharing exactly one vertex, if they contain integers $a$ and $b$ then at least one of the cells sharing a common side with both $A$ and $B$ contains an integer between $a$ and $b$.

We are given an acute triangle $ABC$. Point $D$ lies in the halfplane $AB$ containing $C$ and satisfies $DB\perp AB$ and $\angle ADB=45^\circ+\frac{1}{2}\angle ACB$. Similarly, $E$ lies in the halfplane $AC$ containing $B$ and satisfies $AC\perp EC$ and $\angle AEC=45^\circ+\frac{1}{2}\angle ABC$. Let $F$ be the reflection of $A$ in the midpoint of arc $BAC$ (containing point $A$). Prove that points $A$, $D$, $E$, $F$ are concyclic.
Find all functions $f\colon(0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ such that for all $x,y\in(0,\infty)$ it holds that $$f(x+yf(x))=f(x)f(x+y).$$

In a sequence $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_{100}$ of $100$ mutually different real numbers, we say that an index $i \in \{2, 3, \ldots, 99\}$ is good if $a_1 + \cdots + a_{i-1} = a_{i+1} + \cdots + a_{100}$. What is the largest possible number of good indices?

A positive integer $k$ is called divisive if there exist only finitely many quadruples $(x, y, z, w)$ of positive integers satisfying $$x^2 + y^2 + z^2 + w^2 = xyzw \qquad\text{and}\qquad k \nmid x^2 + y^2 + z^2 + w^2.$$ Find all divisive positive integers.

Let $ABCD$ be a quadrilateral possessing an incenter $I$. Points $K$ and $L$ are chosen on the segments $IA$ and $IC$, respectively, such that $CK \perp ID$ and $AL \perp IB$. Points $P$ and $Q$ are chosen on the segments $AD$ and $BC$, respectively, such that $\angle AKP = \angle ICD$ and $\angle CLQ = \angle IAB$. Prove that $IP = IQ$.

Tom and Jerry play the following game on a $16 \times 16$ chessboard. Jerry starts by selecting some, but not all of the squares, and placing one red pebble on each of the selected squares. Tom then places his one black pebble on an empty square and chooses whether he wants to be the hunter or the prey. After that, Tom and Jerry alternate turns with Jerry starting. In each turn, a player chooses one of his pebbles and moves it to a square sharing an edge with the current square. If such a turn would move the pebble outside of the board, the pebble appears on the other side of the board (i.e. if the pebble is on the left border, it appears in the same row on the right border and similarly for the other cases). If at any point in the game a pebble of the hunter is on the same square as a pebble of the prey, the hunter wins and the game ends. An infinite game is a win for the prey. Which of the two players has a winning strategy?

Let $M$ be the midpoint of side $AD$ of a cyclic quadrilateral $ABCD$. Points $K$ and $L$ are chosen on the rays $MB$ and $MC$ respectively such that $\angle DAK + \angle ACM = \angle ABM$ and $\angle LDA + \angle MBD = \angle MCD$. Prove that the points $B$, $C$, $K$, and $L$ lie on one circle.

Let $n \ge 2$ be an integer and let $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$ be non-zero real numbers such that $$a_1 + \frac{1}{a_2},\quad a_2 + \frac{1}{a_3},\quad \ldots,\quad a_{n-1} + \frac{1}{a_n},\quad a_n + \frac{1}{a_1}$$ are all integers. Prove that $$a_1a_2\ldots a_n + \frac{1}{a_1a_2\ldots a_n}$$ is also an integer.
